newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Bombay gropes for switch after power cut.
newsitem.headline: India's Bombay gropes for switch after power cut.

text.p: Power returned in stages to India's commercial capital of Bombay after it was hit by a sudden widespread failure on Friday.

"We expect power to be restored everywhere by midnight," a spokesman for the state-run Maharashtra State Electricity Board (MSEB) told Reuters. "We haven't yet identified exactly which power stations are not working."
He said that India's entire western state of Maharashtra, where Bombay is located, had been plunged into darkness when a power-station just outside Bombay tripped.
Earlier, state police officials told Reuters that the districts of Bombay, Thane and adjoining Nagpur had been blacked-out.

"Despite the failure, half the state's power stations are still working," the MSEB spokesman said. "We are restoring power to the city gradually -- first the railways, then the hospitals, homes and offices, and so on."
Hundreds of people on their way home from work were stranded when the trains stopped abruptly, railway officials said.
"It's a grid failure. Trains all over Maharashtra have stopped in their tracks," a spokesman for the Central Railway suburban network told Reuters.
A spokesman for BSES Ltd., which provides the bulk of Bombay's power, said supply had not been affected in most of the northwestern suburbs.
Banks, brokerages and the offices of major newspapers, busy analysing the country's budget for 1997/98 (April-March) delivered a few hours earlier, had to stop work.
"We are in darkness but we see light in the stockmarkets," said at a dealer at a foreign brokerage, referring to the provisions of the budget, widely seen as market-friendly.

Power failures are common in India because the country's crumbling infrastructure is unable to satisfy the demand for energy which has multiplied many times since free market reforms began to transform the economy in 1991.
Late in January, the seniormost civil servant in the nation's power ministry warned of the prospect of energy riots as the power shortage took on alarming proportions.

There are frequent blackouts even in the capital New Delhi, and across the country peak shortage is at an average 18 percent. High transmission and distribution losses also contribute to the shortage.
Power Minister S Venugopalachari has estimated that power shortages cost industry $2.7 billion annually, equivalent to 1.5 percent of the gross domestic product.
To offset the shortfall, he recently said, India needed around 100,000 MW of additional capacity involving an investment of four trillion rupees ($112 billion) over the next ten years.
